worksheet.title: Forward and Back
worksheet.subtitle: Forward adds, back takes away
worksheet.learning_goal: I can run a code that mixes forward and back blocks.

parts.title: Two kinds of moves
parts.text: A forward block moves Bit UP the path (it adds steps). A back block moves Bit DOWN the path (it takes steps away). A code can use both. Run the blocks in order, one at a time, to find where Bit lands.

parts.title: Run Code A
parts.prompt: Start on 1. Forward 3, then back 1. Run it one block at a time. What number does Bit land on?

parts.title: Predict, then run Code B
parts.prompt: PREDICT where Bit will land. Then run Code B from 3: forward 1, then back 2. What number does Bit land on?

parts.title: Build C — start at 2, reach 4
parts.note: Use ONE forward block and ONE back block.

parts.title: You try — mix the moves
parts.prompt: Fill the 2 empty blocks with one forward and one back block so Bit goes from 2 to 4. Run it to check. What did you use?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Forward adds steps and back takes steps away — just like adding and subtracting. A code can mix forward and back blocks to reach a number.

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students run programs that mix forward (add) and back (subtract) blocks and write one of their own, connecting sequential code to adding and subtracting within 10. This is reading/running and writing code for a mathematical situation (C3.1) with a predict-and-check step (C3.2).

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 1 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: a floor number path 0-5 so students can step forward and back to feel adding and taking away.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: run Code A — 'start at 1… forward 3 to 4… back 1 to 3.' Name it: forward adds, back takes away.
2. WE DO: Exercise 1 — Code A lands on 3. Exercise 2 — predict Code B, then run: forward 1 to 4, back 2 to 2.
3. YOU DO: Exercise 3 — from 2, use one forward and one back block to reach 4 (e.g. forward 3, back 1).
4. Connect: 'Forward is like adding and back is like subtracting — coding the number path is doing math.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 3 — start 2 → 4: e.g. forward 3, back 1 (net forward 2). Other mixes that net +2 also work, e.g. forward 2 then back 0 is not allowed (no back-0 block), so forward 3/back 1 is the clean pair.
Why it works: each block runs in order; forward adds its number and back subtracts its number, so the landing is start + forwards − backs (kept on the 0-5 path).

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip: treating a back block as forward — point the back arrow/word and step the wrong way once to contrast.
Simplify: do Codes A and B only; skip the build task.
Extend: ask for a program from 2 to 4 that uses a back block first (e.g. back 1 to 1, then forward 3 to 4).
Success indicator: the child lands Code A on 3 and Code B on 2 and writes a forward+back program that reaches 4.
